strengths: Well-motivated and timely problem: instance-level, physically interactive 3D tabletop scene generation for embodied AI/robot manipulation is an important and relatively under-served setting compared to large-scale indoor scene generation, and the paper articulates three concrete criteria (interactive high-quality instances, functionally-semantic layout, precise physically-plausible spatial relations) that ground the evaluation.

The DRO (Differentiable Rotation Optimizer) with a tri-modal (silhouette/edge/appearance) loss and the TSA (Top-view Spatial Alignment) with the RMA-Score anchor selection are sensible, non-trivial technical contributions that directly target the single-view pose/scale ambiguity that limits prior compositional methods; the decoupling of rotation from translation/scale is a reasonable design.

Empirical results are strong and consistent across complementary metrics: best LPIPS/DINOv2/CLIP, dramatically lower collision rates (Col.O 0.42% vs 8-17%, Col.S 7.69% vs 67-98%), and a large human user study (128 participants, 83.13% overall preference) that corroborates the quantitative gains.

Ablations on DRO and TSA (Table 3, Fig. 4) meaningfully isolate each component's effect, and the visualizations clearly show the failure modes (incorrect rotations, misplaced/scaled instances, interpenetration) removed by the full model.

The framework is extended beyond the core setting with real-world image reconstruction, scene editing (object swap preserving layout), stylized/cartoon inputs, and Isaac Sim manipulation demos, demonstrating practical utility and generality.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: implementation details, hyperparameters (lambda weights, tau, optimization settings), and the complete prompt templates are provided in the supplementary, and the paper honestly discusses the fairness caveats of the camera-sweep/best-view selection protocol.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely orchestrational: the pipeline composes off-the-shelf components (GPT-4/ChatGPT for MLLM reasoning, GroundedSAM-v2 for segmentation, Seedream for generative completion and top-view synthesis, Hunyuan3D-3.0 for image-to-3D, PyTorch3D, Isaac Sim), with the main technical novelty concentrated in the DRO/TSA stage. This is acceptable for an applied/systems contribution, but the reliance on MLLM heuristics (camera perspective estimation, commonsense size priors, stacking-order and canonical-axis inference) makes the core reasoning stages somewhat brittle and hard to characterize theoretically.

Missing/limited baselines: the most directly comparable compositional 3D scene generation methods cited in the paper (e.g., CAST and REPARO) are not compared quantitatively; the chosen baselines (ACDC, Gen3DSR, MIDI) are general single-image scene reconstruction methods not specialized for tabletops, so the headline superiority may partly reflect a mismatch in task specialization rather than a strictly fair comparison. Text-to-scene comparison to MesaTask is only qualitative.

The quantitative evaluation set is small (78 scenes), and the collision-rate comparison is arguably favorable to the proposed method by construction, since the pipeline explicitly assembles instances in a physics simulator with collision properties; the definition/measurement of collisions may not be equivalent across methods.

Efficiency is a practical limitation: ~32 minutes per 9-instance scene on an RTX 4090, with the DRO (8-angle coarse search + 140 Adam steps per instance) and image-to-3D stages dominating; the method as presented does not scale well, and full parallelism is left to future work.

The method assumes rotation about the vertical axis only and a single flat support surface, which simplifies tabletop layouts but limits generality (acknowledged in future work); reliance on a synthesized top-view image for translation/scale could compound generative errors, and the anchor-based global scaling is a single-point-of-failure heuristic.

Some methodological circularity concern: GPT-4o is used both as the reasoning MLLM within the pipeline and as the automatic evaluator (GPT Evaluation in Table 1), which risks correlated bias between generation and scoring; the human study mitigates this but does not fully resolve it.

strengths: Targets an important and underexplored problem: instance-level, physically plausible, simulation-ready 3D tabletop scene generation for embodied AI/data synthesis. The paper explicitly distills three sensible criteria (interactive high-quality instances, functionally-semantic layout, precise and physically plausible spatial relations) and evaluates against them, which gives the work a clear purpose beyond generic scene generation.

The pose and scale alignment stage is the most substantive technical contribution and is well designed: the DRO tri-modal loss (soft-IoU silhouette + one-sided Chamfer edge + DINOv2 perceptual) is a reasonable way to recover rotation under single-view ambiguity, and the TSA top-view synthesis with the Ratio-Matched and Area-Weighted Score (RMA-Score) for anchor selection and metric scale recovery is a clean, well-motivated idea. Fig. 11 and Figs. 13-14 make the mechanism concrete.

The ablation is convincing and directly supports the design claims: Table 3 and Fig. 4 show that removing DRO or TSA degrades all visual/perceptual metrics and, more importantly, raises object-level collision rates from 0.42% to 1.27% / 5.50% (and 5.41% with both removed), with the qualitative failure modes (yellow circles, blue parallelograms, red rectangles) matching the numbers.

The empirical evidence is broad and complementary: best LPIPS/DINOv2/CLIP (Table 1), GPT-4o VF/IA/PP and overall ranking, and a dramatically lower collision rate (0.42% object-level, 7.69% scene-level vs 8.23-17.39% / 67.95-98.72% for ACDC/Gen3DSR/MIDI). The collision result is the strongest and most task-relevant signal, since physical plausibility is the stated bottleneck of prior work.

The user study is a real strength rather than a checkbox: 128 participants (126 valid after filtering), randomized result ordering, 7-point scales on three criteria plus forced overall preference, with 83.13% OP for the proposed method. The supplementary documents the survey instrument (Figs. 17-19), which makes the protocol auditable.

Unusually thoughtful fairness analysis in the supplementary: the 160-view camera-sweep protocol with best-view selection, and the argument (Fig. 15b) that this protocol systematically favors baselines by letting an artificially favorable viewpoint mask floating/interpenetrating objects. This is a genuine attempt to avoid overstating the advantage rather than a boilerplate limitations paragraph.

Demonstrated practical extensibility that strengthens the applied case: real-world photo input (Fig. 6), modular instance-level scene editing that preserves the global layout (Fig. 7), style-agnostic generation from cartoon input (Fig. 16), and an actual Franka Panda pick-and-place demonstration in Isaac Sim (Sec. 7) showing the scenes are usable for manipulation tasks, not just visually plausible.

Reproducibility support is good for a training-free pipeline: all prompt templates are released (Figs. 20-25), stage-wise intermediate outputs are shown (Figs. 8-14), and a per-stage efficiency breakdown (~32 min/scene, with timings for extraction, generation, DRO, TSA) is provided along with a stated intent to release code.
weaknesses: The pipeline is largely an integration of off-the-shelf components (ChatGPT for reasoning, Seedream for image synthesis/completion/top-view, GroundedSAM-v2 for segmentation, Hunyuan3D-3.0 for image-to-3D). The genuine technical novelty is concentrated in the DRO/TSA alignment stage; the abstract and introduction frame the result as broadly 'state-of-the-art', which overstates the methodological advance relative to the engineering contribution. The framing should be tightened to match what is actually new.

The quantitative comparison is narrower than the claims suggest. The test set is only 78 samples, and all three quantitative baselines (ACDC, Gen3DSR, MIDI) are general-purpose single-image reconstruction methods rather than tabletop-specialized systems; the one directly comparable tabletop method (MesaTask) is compared only qualitatively in Fig. 5. The claim of 'markedly surpassing existing methods' is therefore supported against adapted, out-of-domain baselines, which weakens the strength of the SOTA claim even if the comparison is defensible in the absence of better alternatives.

The collision-rate comparison, which carries most of the paper's persuasive weight, is under-specified. Sec. 3.4 states that instances are imported into Isaac Sim as rigid bodies with gravity and friction enabled and convex-decomposition colliders, yet Table 1 reports non-zero Col.O/Col.S for baselines and near-zero for the proposed method. It is not clear whether baselines were assembled under the identical protocol, whether physics settling occurs before measurement (which could itself resolve initial penetrations), or whether colliders are attached identically across methods. Without this detail the headline collision numbers are hard to interpret.

The method depends heavily on MLLM commonsense predictions at nearly every stage (object categories, commonsense physical sizes, camera azimuth/elevation, canonical axis correction, stacking order, layout prompt expansion), but there is no sensitivity or failure-mode analysis of these predictions. Statements such as 'we found experimentally that typically only the table requires scaling' are anecdotal; an error analysis of when the MLLM size/axis/order predictions fail would substantially strengthen confidence in the framework's robustness.

The GPT-4o evaluation is used as a primary quantitative criterion (VF/IA/PP and Overall Ranking in Table 1), but the evaluation prompt, rating rubric, and rater configuration for this metric are not documented in the paper (the prompts in Figs. 20-25 cover pipeline stages, not the evaluator). A model-based judge with undisclosed instructions, evaluating rendered images produced by the authors' own rendering setup, is a weak evidentiary basis for a headline claim, and the bias direction is not analyzed.

Efficiency limits the stated use case. At ~32 minutes per scene on a single RTX 4090, with ~830 s for image-to-3D and ~810 s for DRO, and most per-instance stages executed sequentially, the framework is far from the throughput one would want for 'large-scale generation' of training data. The paper acknowledges this and points to future parallelization, but the current cost profile should be weighed against the data-synthesis motivation.

Some reported gains are marginal or metric-dependent: LPIPS improves only from 0.4559 (MIDI) to 0.4483, and the largest margins appear in self-computed collision rates and model-judged scores. The qualitative comparison in Fig. 3 is helpful but is shown for a limited number of tabletop types, so the practical size of the advantage over the strongest baseline is somewhat uncertain.

Reproducibility is constrained by reliance on proprietary or gated models (ChatGPT, Seedream) that may change or become unavailable, which limits the value of the promised code release for exact reproduction. This is a practical constraint rather than a flaw in the science, but it should be stated explicitly as a limitation.

strengths: Problem choice and motivation are strong and well-articulated: tabletop scenes are indeed a bottleneck ('last meter') for manipulation policy learning, and the three distilled criteria (interactive high-quality instances, functionally-semantic layout, precise/physically plausible spatial relations) give a coherent design target and evaluation lens.

The pipeline is a well-engineered, fully automatic, training-free composition of strong pretrained components (MLLM for semantics, GroundedSAM-v2 for segmentation, Seedream for completion, Hunyuan3D-3.0 for image-to-3D, DINOv2/PyTorch3D for the renderer, Isaac Sim for assembly). The 'instance-first, then align' decomposition is sensible and demonstrably yields complete, style-consistent per-instance models (Fig. 10, stylized cartoon input in Fig. 16).

The Differentiable Rotation Optimizer is technically sound and the tri-modal loss (soft-IoU silhouette, one-sided Chamfer edge, DINOv2 perceptual) is a reasonable analysis-by-synthesis formulation; Fig. 11 shows a convincing qualitative match between rendered and reference silhouette/edge/RGB.

The ablation is well designed and informative: removing DRO raises Col_O from 0.42% to 1.27%, removing TSA to 5.50%, removing both to 5.41% (Table 3), with a clear visual diagnosis of the failure modes in Fig. 4 (wrong rotations vs. misplaced/floating objects).

The experimental package is broad: quantitative comparison on LPIPS/DINOv2/CLIP and GPT-4o scoring, collision metrics, a 128-participant user study with randomized display order and bilingual instructions, real-world-photo extension, modular scene editing, efficiency breakdown, robotic pick-and-place demos in Isaac Sim, and full prompt disclosure in the supplementary.

The authors' own analysis of the 'best-view selection' bias (Fig. 15) is commendably honest and technically insightful; it explains why single-view protocols can mask floating/interpenetrating objects and lends credibility to the collision-rate results.

Practical value of the output: scenes are exported as simulation-ready assets with convex-decomposition collision geometry, gravity and friction, and instance-level modularity enables editing without reprocessing the whole scene (Fig. 7).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The system is largely an orchestration of off-the-shelf models; the two advertised novel components are (i) differentiable render-and-compare optimization of a single yaw angle, a long-established analysis-by-synthesis idea, and (ii) an MLLM-heuristic-based translation/scale estimator. No new model, representation, dataset, benchmark, or theory is introduced, so the contribution is closer to a strong systems/application paper than an algorithmic advance.

Core components depend on unvalidated MLLM/diffusion hallucinations. TSA synthesizes a 'perfectly orthographic top-down' image with a generative model and derives all translations from 2D boxes in it, yet nothing verifies that this synthesized view preserves object identity, count, and position relative to the reference image; a diffusion model is not a geometric renderer, and layout errors propagate directly into the 3D scene. Likewise, per-object metric sizes come from GPT commonsense priors (Fig. 22), and the global scale of the entire scene is anchored on a single RMA-selected instance; the paper itself admits the MLLM overestimates the table size. No sensitivity or error analysis of these priors is provided, which is a serious gap for a method whose headline claim is 'precise' pose and scale recovery.

The most relevant prior art, MesaTask (text-driven tabletop generation), is compared only qualitatively (Fig. 5), justified by 'text-based generation lacks consistent reference images.' This is unconvincing: the authors already have a text-to-scene path and image-free evaluation tools (GPT-4o judging, user preference, collision rates) that could be applied to a quantitative comparison. Its absence leaves the 'state-of-the-art' claim unsubstantiated against the closest competitor.

The paper's central motivation — automatic data synthesis for embodied AI and robot policy learning — receives no empirical support. There is no policy-training experiment, no success-rate or data-efficiency comparison, no dataset-scale statistics; the evidence is a qualitative pick-and-place video in the supplementary. For a claim that such scenes are 'essential' for this application, this is anecdotal.

Evaluation protocol concerns. The test set is only 78 self-constructed scenes, not publicly released, and the primary visual metrics (Table 1) use a best-of-160-view selection protocol that the authors themselves demonstrate can mask physical implausibility (Fig. 15). They argue the true gap is larger than reported, but never report the fair multi-view-averaged numbers they evidently possess, so the main quantitative table rests on a protocol of admitted bias.

No variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests anywhere (Tables 1–3 and the user study in Table 2). Several comparisons hinge on small absolute differences (e.g., Col_O 0.42% vs 1.27% in the ablation) reported without any notion of sampling noise.

GPT-4o is used as an automated evaluator (VF/IA/PP/OR) without any validation against human judgment, even though the authors collected human ratings on the same three criteria. Correlating GPT-4o scores with the user study would be a natural sanity check; its absence weakens a substantial portion of the evaluation, and LLM-judge biases (verbosity, order, self-consistency) are not discussed.

The user study, while large, omits essential details: annotator recruitment and expertise, potential conflicts of interest (unpaid volunteers, presumably from the authors' network), inter-annotator agreement, and which view of each method was displayed. The 83.13% overall-preference figure is strong but could partly reflect the rater population and the rendering protocol.

Baseline fairness and the collision metric are under-specified. ACDC (retrieval-based digital cousins), Gen3DSR and MIDI (general single-image scene reconstruction) are not designed for tabletop inputs, and Fig. 3/6 show catastrophic failures (e.g., a single chair or a floating bowl replacing an entire tabletop) that raise the question of whether they were fairly configured (inputs given, camera/hyperparameter tuning). More importantly, it is unclear how collisions are detected (penetration depth? contact? which engine?), and whether all baselines were assembled and settled under the same gravity/physics protocol as the proposed method — the collision metric may favor the proposed pipeline by construction.

No failure-mode or robustness analysis: no reported failure rates for segmentation/completion (which can hallucinate, duplicate, or delete instances), for the MLLM camera-perspective prediction that seeds DRO, for canonical up-axis alignment, or for top-view synthesis. Rotation is estimated only about the vertical axis (yaw); this restriction is neither discussed nor justified as a limitation.

Practical cost and reproducibility: ~32 minutes for a 9-object scene, mostly serial, and heavy dependence on proprietary APIs (GPT-4o, Seedream) conflicts with the stated 'large-scale data synthesis' goal; a code release does not remove this dependence, and no cost/throughput analysis at the scale needed for policy learning is given. Limitations and societal-impact discussion are essentially absent beyond a one-sentence future-work note, and licensing of the reconstructed assets is not addressed.

strengths: Addresses a highly relevant and challenging problem: generating physically plausible, interactive 3D tabletop scenes for robotic manipulation data synthesis, bridging the gap between visual generation and physical executability.

The TabletopGen pipeline effectively integrates multiple advanced foundation models (GroundedSAM-v2, Hunyuan3D, GPT-4, diffusion models) with a novel pose and scale alignment strategy (DRO and TSA) to produce scenes that significantly reduce collisions compared to existing baselines.

Strong experimental validation: The paper provides comprehensive quantitative comparisons (LPIPS, DINOv2, CLIP, GPT-4o evaluations, collision rates), a large-scale user study, and a very compelling zero-shot real-to-sim-to-real transfer demonstration on a physical robot arm.
The ablation studies clearly demonstrate the necessity and contribution of the proposed DRO and TSA modules, particularly regarding physical plausibility and collision avoidance.
High reproducibility: The supplementary material provides a detailed walkthrough of the pipeline, stage-wise outputs, and the exact prompt templates used for LLM/VLM queries.
The paper is well-written and clearly structured, making the complex multi-stage pipeline easy to follow.
weaknesses: The method relies heavily on off-the-shelf foundation models (LLMs, VLMs, Image-to-3D models, diffusion models). While the 'training-free' nature is a strength, the high inference cost, latency, and potential dependency on external API stability are not discussed or quantified.

The core algorithmic novelty is somewhat limited to the orchestration of existing tools (DRO and TSA). The paper does not introduce new foundational architectures or deep learning methods specific to computer vision, making it more of an applied/systems contribution.

The evaluation is limited to single-tabletop surfaces. The authors acknowledge this limitation, but the approach still fails to address multi-level structures (shelves, cabinets) or scenes with highly complex spatial reasoning requirements.

The reliance on LLM/VLM-based spatial reasoning (e.g., determining stacking orders, estimating metric sizes) can be brittle. The paper lacks an in-depth error analysis of cases where the LLM provides incorrect physical priors or spatial commonsense.

Although the zero-shot real-to-sim-to-real transfer achieves significant success, the remaining gaps (e.g., 68% success on the stacking task) are noticeable and primarily attributed to friction and contact modeling, which suggests the generated scenes may still differ physically from the real world.

There is no analysis of the computational overhead (runtime and memory) of the pipeline, which is crucial for evaluating its practicality in generating large-scale synthetic datasets for robotics (one of the paper's primary claims).

strengths: The paper presents a complete, training-free system for converting text or a single image into instance-level interactive tabletop scenes, which is well motivated for robotic manipulation data synthesis.

The proposed DRO and TSA modules are technically sound and address rotation, translation, and scale estimation with differentiable rendering, top-view spatial priors, and physical constraints; ablations support their importance.
The empirical validation is broad: image-driven and text-driven comparisons, GPT-4o evaluation, a 128-participant user study, and zero-shot real-to-sim-to-real policy transfer on a physical robot.

Results are strong across visual fidelity, physical plausibility, and user preference: best LPIPS/DINOv2/CLIP, near-zero collision rates, 83.13% overall user preference, and successful real-world transfer.
The generated scenes are editable and support scene expansion, which adds scalability and practical utility for large-scale embodied AI data generation.
weaknesses: The pipeline relies heavily on multiple off-the-shelf large models and hand-crafted prompts (ChatGPT, Seedream, Hunyuan3D-3.0, GroundedSAM-v2, DINOv2, etc.), raising inference cost, reproducibility, and brittleness concerns despite the 'training-free' framing.

The main evaluation uses a relatively small test set (78 scenes, only 4 real-world photos) and lacks statistical variance or significance testing; GPT-4o and user-study scores are subjective and may be sensitive to prompt and interface design.

Pose and scale estimation depends on generated top-view images and MLLM commonsense size estimates, so it may fail under severe occlusion, transparent/reflective objects, or unusual tabletop configurations; the paper acknowledges only some of these limitations.

Physical plausibility is mainly measured by collision/support metrics, and the real-robot validation covers only three simple tasks, with lower real-world success on stacking, leaving the sim-to-real gap incompletely characterized.

Beyond system integration, the core algorithmic novelty is the DRO and TSA alignment strategy; most components are existing models, so the contribution may be seen as somewhat incremental without additional theoretical or empirical differentiation.

strengths: Targets an important and practical problem: automated generation of simulation-ready 3D tabletop scenes for robot manipulation data synthesis.

Proposes a modular training-free pipeline with two technical components: Differentiable Rotation Optimizer (DRO) and Top-View Spatial Alignment (TSA), combining generative models with geometric/physical priors.

Extensive experiments: quantitative image-driven and text-driven comparisons, ablation of DRO/TSA, collision/visual metrics, user study with 126 valid participants, and zero-shot real-to-sim-to-real transfer on a physical robot.
Good clarity and supplementary details; prompts, implementation details, and additional results are provided.
weaknesses: Method is largely a composition of existing pretrained models (ChatGPT, GroundedSAM-v2, Seedream, Hunyuan3D-3.0, Isaac Sim) and simple losses/priors; the core algorithmic novelty over prior scene-generation pipelines may be limited.

Reliance on MLLM outputs for category recognition, physical size, stacking order, and top-view synthesis introduces potential error propagation; these components are not comprehensively ablated and cannot guarantee collision-free or physically valid layouts.

GPT-4o is used both as part of the generation pipeline and as an automatic evaluator, which risks self-preference and overstates semantic/physical scores; text-driven comparisons lack human validation.
Reproducibility is constrained by proprietary/large external model APIs and nondeterministic MLLM outputs; the paper does not provide code or fully specified versions, though prompts are included.
Real-robot validation is limited to a few pick-and-place tasks and a small set of trials; more complex manipulation and broader real-world settings are needed to fully support the data-engine claim.
